title: Palindrome Partitioning IV
statement: Decide whether the string `s` can be cut into exactly three consecutive pieces, each non-empty, such that every piece reads the same forwards and backwards (a palindrome). Return `true` if some choice of the two cut points works and `false` if none does. The three pieces must cover all of `s` in order.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every pair of cut points is only O(n²) pairs, but checking each piece by reversing it costs another O(n), giving O(n³). The fix is to answer "is `s[i..j]` a palindrome?" in O(1) after a quadratic precomputation. A substring is a palindrome exactly when its two end letters match and the part strictly inside is a palindrome (or is empty or one letter), which is a classic interval DP.

## Approach

1. Build an `n × n` table `isPal`, filling `start` from the right end down so that `isPal[start + 1][end - 1]` is already known.
2. Mark `isPal[start][end]` true when `s[start] === s[end]` and the inside is short (`end - start < 2`) or itself a palindrome.
3. Try every end index `firstEnd` for the first piece; skip it unless `s[0..firstEnd]` is a palindrome.
4. For each end index `secondEnd` of the middle piece, check the middle `s[firstEnd+1..secondEnd]` and the last piece `s[secondEnd+1..n-1]` in the table.
5. Return `true` on the first success; `false` after all pairs fail.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abcbdd"`, `n = 6`. The table marks single letters, `"bcb"` (indices 1–3) and `"dd"` (4–5) among others. With `firstEnd = 0`, the piece `"a"` is a palindrome. `secondEnd = 1` gives middle `"b"` but last `"cbdd"`, which fails; `secondEnd = 2` gives middle `"bc"`, which fails; `secondEnd = 3` gives middle `"bcb"` and last `"dd"`, both palindromes, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): the table has n² cells filled in O(1) each, and the cut pairs are at most n².
- Space: O(n²) for `isPal`.

## Pitfalls

- Fill `start` in decreasing order; going left to right reads cells that are not computed yet.
- Every piece must be non-empty, so `firstEnd` stops before `n - 2` and `secondEnd` before `n - 1`.
- Do not stop at the first palindromic prefix; a longer prefix may be the one that works.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `isPal` | `isPal[start][end]` is true when `s[start..end]` is a palindrome |
| `start`, `end` | inclusive bounds of the substring being classified |
| `firstEnd` | last index of the first piece |
| `secondEnd` | last index of the middle piece |

narration.3: Make an n by n table where isPal[start][end] will say whether s[start..end] is a palindrome.
narration.4: Walk start from the right end so the inner cell isPal[start + 1][end - 1] is always ready.
narration.5: Try every end at or after start.
narration.6: The ends must match, and the inside must be empty, one letter, or already a palindrome.
narration.7: Record that s[start..end] is a palindrome.
narration.11: Choose where the first piece ends, leaving room for two more non-empty pieces.
narration.12: Skip this choice unless the first piece s[0..firstEnd] is a palindrome.
narration.15: Choose where the middle piece ends, leaving at least one letter for the last piece.
narration.16: Check the middle piece and the last piece with two table lookups.
narration.17: All three pieces are palindromes, so a valid split exists.
narration.21: No pair of cut points worked.
